value.overview: The Boat-billed Heron (Cochlearius cochlearius) is a distinctive tropical waterbird named for its unusually broad, flattened bill. Although it belongs to the heron family, it has a compact body, short legs, large eyes, and largely nocturnal habits that give it a different appearance from many typical herons. It usually lives near quiet freshwater, brackish wetlands, mangroves, and forest waterways in tropical parts of Central and South America.
value.classification: The Boat-billed Heron is in the heron family, Ardeidae, and is the only living species in the genus Cochlearius. It is sometimes placed with night herons because of its nocturnal behavior and body form.
value.identification: Adults have a large, dark, scoop-shaped bill that is broad enough to appear almost as wide as the head. The crown and upper back are dark, while the face, neck, and underparts are generally gray to pale gray. The body is stocky, the legs are relatively short, and the eyes are large and adapted to low light. Young birds are browner and less sharply patterned. Its slow wingbeats and unusual silhouette are distinctive.
value.rangeHabitat: The Boat-billed Heron ranges from Mexico through Central America and much of tropical South America. In Costa Rica it occurs in suitable lowland wetlands on both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes, including mangrove forests, river edges, marshes, lagoons, swamps, and densely vegetated waterways. It is associated mainly with coastal and near-coastal lowlands, although it may also use inland wetland habitats. Important Costa Rican areas for the species include Tortuguero, Corcovado, Palo Verde, and other protected wetland landscapes.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally resident and rather sedentary. In Costa Rica, Boat-billed Herons are considered year-round birds rather than regular long-distance migrants, although local movements between roosting, nesting, freshwater, and tidal feeding sites may occur.
value.breeding: Boat-billed Herons nest singly or in small colonies, usually in trees, shrubs, reed beds, or other vegetation above or close to water. Both adults help build the nest, incubate the eggs, and feed the young. Clutches commonly contain two or three pale bluish eggs. The chicks hatch dependent on their parents and remain in or near the nest for several weeks. Breeding may be colonial where suitable wetland nesting habitat is concentrated.
value.dietFeeding: The diet includes small fish, crustaceans, aquatic insects, worms, frogs, and other small wetland animals. Feeding is mainly nocturnal, when the heron moves quietly along shallow water, muddy edges, or branches overhanging channels. Its broad bill can be used to seize prey from the water or vegetation, and tactile feeding may help it detect prey in dark or turbid conditions.
value.behavior: During the day, Boat-billed Herons usually roost quietly in dense vegetation, often alone or in groups. They become more active after dusk and may produce harsh, croaking or squawking calls. Birds may gather communally at roosts, while feeding is often more dispersed. Courtship includes crest raising, bill movements, and vocal or chattering displays. Their secretive habits and nocturnal activity can make them easy to overlook even where they are established.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable.
